Rabbi Yitzhak Alfiyah: A Central Figure in the World of Kabbalah and Sephardic Leadership in Jerusalem

This text surveys the life and spiritual contribution of Rabbi Yitzhak Alfiyah, a central figure in the world of Kabbalah and Sephardic leadership in Jerusalem during the first half of the twentieth century. The article traces his life trajectory from his childhood in Aram Tzova to his ascent to the "Beit El" yeshiva, while emphasizing the extreme humility that characterized him alongside his profound expertise in the esoteric Torah. The central axis of the writing deals with his innovative public enterprises, primarily the establishment of "Ta'anit HaDibur" (the Fast of Speech) as a spiritual substitute for physical fasting and the founding of the "Or Ḥadash" (New Light) society which sought to make Torah study accessible to all strata of the people. Through detailing his Torah compositions and his confrontation with events during the Mandatory period and the War of Independence, the source presents the rabbi as a living bridge between the preservation of ancient traditions and active leadership seeking to repair society and arouse heavenly mercy upon Israel.

The Doctrine and Activity of the Kabbalist Rabbi Yitzhak Alfiyah: A Central Figure in the World of Kabbalah and Sephardic Leadership in Jerusalem

The figure of the kabbalist Rabbi Yitzhak Alfiyah represents a glorious and multi-layered chapter in the history of the Jewish Yishuv in the Land of Israel in general, and in the history of the Sephardic sages of Jerusalem in particular. His activity, spanning the first half of the twentieth century, is not limited to the four cubits of the kabbalists' yeshiva "Beit El," but rather bursts into the public sphere through social reforms, innovative educational initiatives, and spiritual leadership that sought to bridge between the revealed world and the hidden world, and between the conservative tradition of the Aram Tzova community and the changing reality in Mandatory Palestine and the early days of the State.[1, 2, 3]

Family Roots and the Formation of Spiritual Identity in Aram Tzova

Rabbi Yitzhak Alfiyah was born on the 18th of Shevat 5638 (1878) in the city of Aleppo, known by its traditional name Aram Tzova, in Syria.[1, 2, 3] This community, renowned for its adherence to ancient customs and profound scholarship, served as his first intellectual nursery. His father, the kabbalist Rabbi Ya'akov Ḥayim Yisrael Refa'el, was a central figure in the kabbalistic world of Aleppo, and his mother Sarah (called Tzalḥa) died when he was only about five years old.[1, 3, 4] His early orphanhood led to his being raised in the home of his paternal grandfather, Rabbi Yitzhak Yesha'yah Alfiyah, after whom he was named.[1, 2, 3]

The grandfather's influence on his grandson was decisive. The grandfather not only raised him physically, but also shaped his Torah and halakhic outlook, and even ordained him for ritual slaughter—a profession that served Rabbi Alfiyah as a modest source of livelihood for many years, out of a desire to remain independent of the public purse.[1, 2, 3] Rabbi Alfiyah's family structure was broad and ramified, and included his brothers Rabbi Yesha'yah Sha'ul and Rabbi Mordekhai Mosheh, and his half-sister Tzalḥa.[1, 4]

Integration in Jerusalem and the Connection with the "Beit El" Yeshiva

Upon his immigration to Jerusalem, Rabbi Alfiyah settled in the Old City, the very heart of spiritual existence in Israel at that time. He began his studies at the kabbalists' yeshiva "Beit El," an institution that constituted the world center for the dissemination of the Torah of the RaSHaSH (Rabbi Shalom Sharabi) and the kavanot (mystical intentions) of the ARI.[1, 3, 5] In this yeshiva, Rabbi Alfiyah was exposed to the most rigorous speculative and practical kabbalistic tradition, emphasizing the power of concentrated prayer and the importance of spiritual repairs (tikkunim) for the redemption of the Shekhinah.[6]

Despite his recognized greatness in both revealed and hidden Torah, Rabbi Alfiyah was distinguished by extreme humility. In the introduction to his book he describes himself in these words: "If in the wisdom of peshat my intellect is too limited to understand, how much more so and all the more so is this true for me in its secrets and in the wisdom of Kabbalah and the supernal mysteries therein."[1] He claimed that the title "ḥakham" attached to him was merely a tribute of honor to his late grandfather.[1] This humility did not prevent him from becoming one of the greatest kabbalists of his generation, when students such as Rabbi Menaḥem Menasheh and the kabbalist Rabbi Ovadyah Hedayah, author of Yaskil Avdi, saw in him a supreme spiritual authority.[1]

His relationship with Rabbi Ovadyah Hedayah is particularly significant for understanding the spiritual network in Jerusalem. Both operated within the tradition of the "Beit El" yeshiva, which constituted a central axis of esoteric Kabbalah focused on the kavanot of the RaSHaSH.[6] They were part of a vibrant center of kabbalistic life in Jerusalem, which stood in contrast to certain historiographic conceptions that viewed Kabbalah at that time as a "dying ember."[6] Their joint activity included dissemination of tikkunim, prayers, and customs literature among the broad public, while making the esoteric accessible to the masses in a controlled manner.[6]

Public Activity and the Establishment of the "Or Ḥadash Ve-Tzemaḥ Tzedek" Society

In the year 5667 (1907) Rabbi Alfiyah was called to serve as a member of the rabbinical court in Jerusalem, a prestigious position by all accounts.[1, 2, 3] However, after a short period he chose to resign from his official position, apparently out of a desire to dedicate his time to freer public activity and personal study far from the formal rabbinic establishment.[1, 2, 3]

In the year 5680 (1920) he founded together with other rabbis the "Or-Ḥadash Ve-Tzemaḥ-Tzedek" society.[1] The society's center was established in the synagogue of the "Misgav Ladakh" hospital in the Old City.[1, 2, 3] The society's purpose was revolutionary for its time: creating a framework for joint Torah study intended for Jews from all strata of the population—from great Torah scholars to simple craftsmen.[1, 2, 3] Rabbi Alfiyah personally attended to all the yeshiva's needs, from fundraising to providing for the students' sustenance. In this context his moral scrupulousness stood out; he refused to accept donations from people who were not Shabbat observers, out of a conception that purity of funds was essential to the sanctity of study.[1]

The society engaged not only in theoretical study but also in social and spiritual repair. Rabbi Alfiyah organized Torah scholars who engaged in Kabbalah at the "Beit El" yeshiva and provided for their salaries, thereby ensuring the continuation of the RaSHaSH tradition in Jerusalem.[1] The society's regulations and letters of support for it, which were published later, attest to the great esteem it enjoyed from public figures and rabbis of all communities.[7]

The Stay in Rishon LeZion Colony and the "Olei Regel" Society

A fascinating chapter in Rabbi Alfiyah's life occurred in the year 5671 (1911), when he moved to reside in the Rishon LeZion colony.[1, 2, 3] The move from the enclosed Old City to one of Zionism's first colonies symbolizes his willingness to operate in new spaces. In this colony he founded the "Olei Regel" (Pilgrims) society, a group numbering about 50 members who were meticulous about ascending to Jerusalem for each festival to fulfill the remembrance of the commandment of pilgrimage.[1, 2, 3] This initiative sought to strengthen the connection between the new Yishuv and the spiritual center in Jerusalem.

For four years Rabbi Alfiyah served as a teacher (melamed) for boys in the local school in Rishon LeZion.[1] However, when it became known to him that the school was financially supported by elements defined as "secular" (apparently organizations that promoted free education), he took an unprecedented step: he resigned from his position and returned all the salary he had received over four years, despite his straitened economic situation.[1] This action demonstrates his unwillingness to compromise on the independence of Torah education and the moral precision he demanded of himself.

The "Ta'anit HaDibur" Enterprise and His Ethical-Kabbalistic Doctrine

The contribution most identified today with Rabbi Yitzhak Alfiyah to the Jewish world is the dissemination of the concept "ta'anit dibur" (fast of speech).[2, 8] Although the custom was mentioned in early sources, Rabbi Alfiyah was the one who transformed it into a mass movement and arranged for it the orders of prayer and study accepted today.[8, 9]

The Philosophy Behind Silence

Rabbi Alfiyah held that in recent generations bodily powers have weakened, and observing physical fasts could lead to neglect of Torah or harm to health.[9, 10] In contrast, the fast of speech—complete abstention from mundane speech and dedication of the mouth to Torah study and prayer—is considered by him a greater repair.[8, 9] He claimed that the mouth, which constitutes a source for social and spiritual sins (l
lashon hara, falsehood, obscene speech), is the instrument through which the rectification must be accomplished: "not to take in food—and not to emit mundane speech."[10]

According to his teaching, the fast of speech possesses special segulah value when observed communally.[9] He disseminated the idea that these fasts should be observed especially during the days of Shovavim (the weeks when the Torah portions from Exodus through Mishpatim are read), a period traditionally designated for the rectification of sins.[8, 11] Additionally, he emphasized the superior merit of the fast of speech on the Sabbath day, since on the Sabbath it is more severe to speak forbidden speech than on a weekday.[9] The custom generally includes the recitation of the entire book of Psalms three times consecutively, an action perceived as possessing tremendous expiatory power.[9]

Global Dissemination and the Sanigoryah Prayer

Thanks to his efforts, the custom spread from Jerusalem to numerous Jewish communities throughout the world.[8] Rabbi Alfia composed a special "Sanigoryah prayer" recited before the open ark during the fast days.[2, 12] This prayer is intended to arouse heavenly mercy upon the people of Israel, while emphasizing Israel's merits against the accusers. Rabbi Nissim Peretz of blessed memory, among the great kabbalists of the last generation, would recite this prayer with great emotion in the study hall of the "Beit El" institutions in Bnei Brak, adding personal supplications, thereby continuing Rabbi Alfia's legacy.[12]

His Literary Oeuvre: Between Nigleh and Nistar

The books of Rabbi Yitzhak Alfia constitute a mosaic of his Torah thought. Many of them were printed in first editions in Jerusalem and received approbations and praise from the great scholars of the generation.[5]

Kuntres HaYechi'eli (1928): A three-part book dealing with practical halakhah and spiritual practices.[5] It discusses the honor due to the synagogue, laws of mezuzah, parapet, terumot and ma'aserot, and laws of burial and mourning.[5, 13] The book reflects his scrupulous attention to the finest detail in customs and the conduct of the Jewish home.

Siach Yitzhak (1923): This work is divided into two parts; the first part includes special prayers at the graves of tzaddikim, petitions and tikkkunim, and the second part contains Torah novellae and homilies.[2, 3, 14]

Ya'ir Nativ (1939): In this work Rabbi Alfia explained the merit and order of study of "Torah lishmah" in groups of ten.[5] He established a structured curriculum integrating most of the foundational works of Judaism, with the aim of creating broad proficiency among students.[2, 5]

Ahavat HaShem (1943): This book addresses the preservation of Jewish customs and the absolute prohibition against following the ways of the nations.[3, 5, 14] Rabbi Alfia regarded the alteration of customs as an existential spiritual danger, and based his words on sources from the Zohar, the Talmud, and the Midrashim.[3, 5] The book also focuses on funeral and mourning customs, warning against the adoption of modern-secular behavioral patterns.[3]

Re'ach LeYitzhak (1934): A collection of kabbalistic teachings including homilies and rulings from his father, the kabbalist Rabbi Ya'akov Alfia.[5, 13, 14] Through this book Rabbi Alfia preserved his family's Torah and transmitted it to the broader public.

Or Chadash and Tzemach Tzaddik: A book detailing the orders of the fast of speech, its merits and the segulot of Psalms, alongside homilies and responsa correspondence.[13, 14, 15]

Formative Events and Historical Context

Rabbi Alfia's life was not free from geopolitical upheavals. During World War II, following a dream he had, he embarked on an extraordinary journey to Egypt.[1, 2] He obtained permission from the military governor and traveled by military train to pray at the grave of the tzaddik Rabbi Ya'akov Abuhatzeira (author of Machshof HaLavan), out of faith that this prayer would stand in merit of the people of Israel in their difficult hours.[1, 2]

The Tragedy of 1948 and the Loss of Manuscripts

The most severe blow on both the personal and Torah planes befell him in the year 1948.[14] During the battle for the Jewish Quarter in the Old City, Rabbi Alfia acted in a desperate attempt to keep ten Jewish families in the Quarter under Jordanian rule, motivated by the desire to preserve the Jewish settlement in the holy place.[2, 14] The attempt failed, and he was exiled together with the rest of the Quarter's residents to the new neighborhoods of Jerusalem.[1, 2, 14]

During the evacuation and transition, most of his manuscripts and unpublished works were lost.[1, 2, 14] This is a significant historical loss, as a substantial portion of his kabbalistic and halakhic teaching that had been preserved in manuscript vanished forever.[14] Only the books that had already appeared in print beforehand survived and became the foundation of his legacy.

Relations with the Sages of His Generation and His Worldview

Rabbi Alfia was an integral part of Jerusalem's spiritual elite. He gathered many kabbalists around him and even provided for their salaries from donations.[1] His influence reached Rabbi Mordechai Eliyahu of blessed memory, who related that his father (Rabbi Salman Eliyahu) regarded Rabbi Alfia as one of the thirty-six hidden righteous of the generation.[2]

In the political and national sphere, his kabbalistic teaching at times provided interpretation for modern processes. Although he maintained a stringently conservative line in matters of custom, his connections with figures such as Rabbi Ovadiah Hadaya show that in the Jerusalem kabbalistic world of that period, there was room for conferring "divine-messianic" validity upon the processes of the return to Zion, while addressing the challenges of technology and secularism through the prism of the practices of the Rashash.[6]

His homilies, dealing with love of Israel, charity, and kindness, emphasize the importance of the people's unity.[13] He taught that charity called "a little" extinguishes great transgression, as it is written "yet a little while, and the wicked shall not be," thereby emphasizing the value of every small good deed.[13]

His Final Days and His Legacy for Generations

Rabbi Yitzhak Alfia passed away on September 13, 1955 (26 Elul 5715) after an illness.[2] He was buried in the rabbinical section of Har HaMenuchot in Jerusalem.[2] After his passing, a fund was established for the publication of his books, which worked to preserve and disseminate his remaining writings.[2, 3]

His legacy lives today through thousands of Jews who observe the global "fast of speech" each year, and through study halls that continue to study according to his methods.[8, 12] He remains a symbol of a leader who combined personal asceticism and supreme holiness with deep and simple concern for every Jew, while standing firm in safeguarding tradition and custom.

The Torah teaching of Rabbi Alfia instructs that precisely through silence and self-restraint can a person reach high spiritual levels and influence physical and political reality. His insistence on the boundaries of custom and preservation of the Aram Tzova tradition in Jerusalem erected a barrier against processes of cultural assimilation, and provided Sephardic Jewry with a powerful tool for religious renewal without losing its ancient roots. His work in making kabbalah accessible through practical tikkunim and egalitarian study made him one of the most influential figures in shaping Sephardic religiosity in the twentieth century.
